subject: penguin
reasoning:
I need to build a penguin model using the three.js SDK, keeping it compact but visually solid, while sticking strictly to the documented builder APIs available to me.

Planning the skeleton: hips joint near the base, a spine chain leading up to the neck, with the body shaped as a stubby ellipsoid using scaled parts for the black back and white belly.

Building out the joint hierarchy...

Legs get a simple joint chain with a small flat foot sphere scaled into a paddle shape, parented appropriately and colored orange to contrast with the black and white body.

Now I'm laying out the body geometry: a black ellipsoid back and a smaller white belly ellipsoid offset forward, a round head with a white face patch, tiny eyes with black pupils, and I'm figuring out how to orient a cone for the beak since the geometry's default axis may not match the direction I need it to point.

I decide to avoid aim-direction uncertainty by baking the rotation directly into the cone geometry so it points along +Z, then split the beak into upper and lower jaw parts attached to separate head and jaw bones. For the flippers, I'm planning shoulder joints with scaled sphere geometry rotated to splay outward, working through which side needs positive or negative tilt.

I also want to make the penguin less generic by adding a tuxedo belly, eyes, orange ear patches for a king/emperor penguin look, and simple feet, while skipping risky patterned surface painting. I'm working out the vertical positioning so legs, feet, and hips line up correctly relative to the body's bottom edge.

Now I'm sketching out the leg cylinders, checking overall height against real penguin proportions and settling on a stylized ~0.6-0.7m scale, then confirming the feet rest exactly at ground level. I'm also planning how joints and parented bones should reference each other, and starting to lay out the sphere-based head, eyes, and pupils with their positions and scales.

I'm skipping unnecessary imports like a random generator, adding the meta export with name and description, then working through the beak geometry—placing jaw and upper/lower beak cones with rotation and offsets so the tip points outward and slightly downward.
